questions.topic: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
questions.learningObjective: Describe the categories that begin a case in the Supreme Court.
questions.stem: In a site selection memo, the planner asks what the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction consists of. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: The Court's original jurisdiction covers a short list of defined controversies, chiefly disputes between two or more states and suits against a state brought by citizens of another state or of a foreign country, together with suits by a state against citizens of another state. Its broader role is reviewing decisions of the lower courts, and that appellate work is the great majority of what the Court decides each term, so original matters form only a small part of the docket.

questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction is a short, defined list, while the Court's main work is reviewing lower court decisions. Ordinary municipal and contract disputes do not begin there.
questions.hint: Recall the short list of cases that begin in the Court.

questions.topic: Discretionary review and denial of review
questions.learningObjective: Explain the legal effect of a denial of review.

stimulus.body: A case handling note describes the Supreme Court's petition process. It states that a party seeking review of a lower court decision files a petition asking the Court to review that decision and to grant the petition, that most petitions are denied without a written opinion, and that a denial of review does not mean the Court agreed with the decision below, only that the Court chose not to decide the case.

options.misconception: reads a denial as an endorsement of the decision

options.text: A denial of review is published with a full explanation in most cases
options.misconception: ignores that most denials carry no opinion

options.text: A petition that is denied must be refiled in a state court for another hearing
options.misconception: invents a state remand after a denial

options.text: A denial of review leaves the lower decision standing without endorsing it

questions.explanation: The note says denials are common, usually without an opinion, and carry no agreement with the decision below. The lower ruling simply stands while the Court declines to decide the case.
questions.hint: Separate declining to review from agreeing with the ruling.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the quorum rule and its effect on decisions.
questions.stem: The planner's memo asks what happens when fewer than nine justices are available to hear a case. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: Six justices constitute a quorum, so the Court can do business with six members, but the Court normally requires nine members to decide a case, and where fewer than nine justices are in office the number needed for a decision rises accordingly, with seven required when eight or fewer justices are available. A missing or recused justice therefore can affect whether a case is heard at all, which is why the Court moves quickly to fill vacancies.

questions.explanation: Six justices form a quorum, but deciding a case normally requires nine, and fewer available justices raises the number needed. Vacancies can therefore slow or prevent decisions.
questions.hint: Separate the quorum for business from the votes needed to decide.

A guilty verdict required ten of the twelve jurors to agree

options.misconception: confuses the verdict with sentencing

questions.explanation: The note describes a twelve person jury that must agree unanimously to convict, with the judge handling sentencing afterwards. Guessing a vote threshold or swapping jury and judge duties contradicts the note.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the work of trial courts from appellate courts.
questions.stem: In a memo about a disputed access route, the planner asks what a trial court does that an appellate court does not. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: A trial court hears witnesses, accepts evidence, and finds facts from that record, and it is this court that decides the case in the first instance. An appellate court does not take new evidence; it reviews the record that the trial court created and asks whether the law was applied correctly or whether the proceedings were unfair, and it then affirms, reverses, or remands without normally deciding the facts anew.

questions.explanation: Trial courts hear evidence and find facts, while appellate courts review that record without hearing witnesses. The appellate court checks the process and the law, then affirms, reverses, or remands.
questions.hint: Separate finding facts from reviewing a record.

stimulus.body: An appellate practice note states that a notice of appeal must be filed within the time allowed by the rules of the relevant court of appeals, that the appeal brings up the trial court's record rather than new evidence, and that the court of appeals may affirm, reverse, or remand. An appeal starts a new trial in which new evidence may be presented

options.text: Every disappointed party may obtain Supreme Court review as of right
options.misconception: ignores the note's statement that a request is rarely granted

options.text: The court of appeals may only affirm a trial court decision, never reverse it
options.misconception: denies the note's list of dispositions

questions.explanation: The note describes review of an existing record with affirm, reverse, or remand as the possible outcomes, and it makes clear that a petition for review is discretionary and rarely granted.
questions.hint: Find what an appeal brings up and what comes after it.

options.misconception: assumes a denial reverses the judgment

options.text: The refusal leaves the loss in place, and the party gains no further remedy from that refusal
The refusal converts the case into a state court matter for a second appeal

options.text: The refusal guarantees the case will be heard later if facts change
options.misconception: invents a guarantee of future review

questions.explanation: Denial of review is discretionary and nonbinding on the merits, so the loss stands and no new remedy arises from the refusal. Only a change in the legal question would create a different case.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the complete diversity rule to corporate parties.
questions.stem: The memo reviews a lease dispute: the plaintiff is incorporated in one state and the defendant is incorporated in another, and both maintain their headquarters in a third state. Which answer best describes federal jurisdiction?

answer.exemplar: Complete diversity requires that every plaintiff be a citizen of a state different from every defendant's state, and a corporation is a citizen of its state of incorporation and the state of its principal place of business. Here each corporation is a citizen of two states, so if those sets of states overlap, the case lacks complete diversity and cannot be heard in federal court on the diversity ground, even though the two named states of incorporation differ.

questions.explanation: Complete diversity requires no shared state of citizenship between any plaintiff and any defendant, and corporations count from both their state of incorporation and their principal place of business.
questions.hint: Check every plaintiff's citizenship against every defendant's.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretionary review and denial of review
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Court grants review of only a small share of cases.
questions.stem: While the planner redrafts the parking code, the log asks why the Court rarely grants review of state court decisions. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: The Court decides a small share of the cases it might review, because it must decide both whether to take a case at all and then how to decide it, and its institutional capacity is limited. It takes cases that settle broad questions of law that many courts and litigants rely on, while denying the many petitions that turn on narrow, fact-bound disputes that lower courts are equipped to resolve and that the Court has no reason to unsettle.

questions.explanation: The Court selects cases that resolve broad legal questions and denies narrow, fact-bound ones, which keeps its docket workable. Capacity, not indifference, drives the small share taken.
questions.hint: Consider which kind of disputes need a national answer.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the requirements for federal jurisdiction over a diversity case.

stimulus.body: A legal note explains that a case between citizens of different states may be heard in federal court only if every plaintiff is a citizen of a state different from every defendant's state, and only if the amount in controversy exceeds 75,000 dollars exclusive of interest and costs. The note adds that corporations are citizens of both their state of incorporation and the state of their principal place of business, that the citizenship of the parties is determined when the complaint is filed, and that a later change does not defeat jurisdiction once established.

questions.stem: Of the statements offered, which one does the note confirm as accurate?

options.text: Corporations are citizens only of the state where they are incorporated
options.misconception: ignores the principal place of business rule

options.text: Interest and attorney fees count toward the 75,000 dollar threshold
options.misconception: reverses the note's exclusion rule

options.text: A case qualifies whenever the plaintiff and the defendant are citizens of different states
options.misconception: misses the complete diversity requirement

options.text: Citizenship is fixed when the complaint is filed, and later changes do not defeat jurisdiction

questions.explanation: The note fixes citizenship at filing, applies complete diversity, excludes interest and costs, and treats corporations as citizens of two states. Only the filing-time rule matches everything the note says.
questions.hint: Match the option to the note's rule about timing.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the practical effect of a vacancy on the Court.
questions.stem: The planner asks why a vacancy can matter beyond leaving a seat empty. Which answer is best?

options.text: Fewer available justices can mean a case cannot be decided, because nine are normally required
A vacancy invalidates all prior decisions of the Court in that term
options.misconception: overstates the effect of a vacancy

options.text: A vacancy causes the Court to hear only cases arising in one state
options.misconception: invents a docket rule tied to vacancies

options.text: A vacancy transfers the seat to the governor of the state in which the case arose
options.misconception: confuses appointment procedures with case assignment

questions.explanation: Because a case normally needs nine members, a vacancy can leave the Court unable to decide, which raises the stakes of appointment. It does not undo prior decisions or reshuffle the docket.
questions.hint: Think about how many justices a decision requires.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the verdict from the sentence that follows.
questions.stem: The planner asks how a jury's verdict differs from the sentence that follows. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: The verdict decides guilt or innocence and is the jury's own judgment on the facts, returned only when the jurors agree unanimously. Sentencing is a separate stage, and in federal criminal cases the judge imposes the sentence after the verdict, guided by the sentencing guidelines and the statute, with the defendant sometimes permitted to argue for a lesser sentence. A juror who disagreed with the penalty had no role in fixing it, which is one reason the two decisions are treated separately.

questions.explanation: The verdict resolves guilt unanimously, while sentencing follows as a separate stage that the judge controls in federal criminal cases. The jury's role does not extend to the penalty.
questions.hint: Separate the finding of guilt from the penalty imposed.

A federal district court, because it reviews decisions made by other district courts

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Court of appeals as intermediate tier
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish vacating a decision from reversing it.
questions.stem: The planner reads that a court of appeals found an agency's explanation inadequate and sent the matter back for a new decision. Which action did the appellate court take?

answer.exemplar: The court of appeals did not substitute its own judgment for the agency's; it set aside the agency's decision and returned the matter for the agency to act again, which is a remand rather than a reversal. A reversal would put a different outcome in place, whereas a vacatur leaves the agency free to redo its reasoning within the limits the court has set, and the choice matters in administrative practice because the agency decides again.

questions.explanation: Sending the matter back without substituting a result is a vacatur and remand, while reversing would put a new outcome in place. The difference matters because the agency decides again.
questions.hint: Separate undoing a decision from replacing it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the pleading requirement for federal question jurisdiction.

stimulus.body: A claims review note explains that a federal trial court hears a case when the plaintiff's claim arises under federal law, and that a federal claim must be stated so that it appears on the face of the complaint rather than only as a defence. The note adds that a federal statute may also provide the court with jurisdiction over a state-law claim, that a claim may be removed from state court only if the federal requirements are satisfied, and that a federal claim is not lost simply because the federal issue fails.

questions.stem: Which of the statements below agrees with the note?

options.text: A federal claim must appear on the face of the complaint to support jurisdiction
A federal issue may be raised for the first time as a defence to support jurisdiction
options.misconception: contradicts the note's pleading requirement

options.text: Federal jurisdiction over a state claim requires the amount in controversy to exceed a threshold
options.misconception: borrows the diversity threshold rule

options.text: Removing a case to federal court requires the consent of the other party
options.misconception: invents a consent requirement the note does not state

questions.explanation: The note ties federal jurisdiction to a federal claim stated on the face of the complaint, and it identifies other routes such as statutes extending jurisdiction over state-law claims. Removal is not a matter of consent.
questions.hint: Read the note's rule about how the claim must be pleaded.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the rule for removing a diversity case to federal court.
questions.stem: The planner asks what happens when a diversity case is filed in state court and one side wants it heard in federal court. Which answer best describes the rule?

options.text: Removal is permitted whenever a party prefers federal court
options.misconception: treats removal as a matter of preference

options.text: A case may be removed to federal court if the federal requirements, including complete diversity, are satisfied
The case must stay in state court unless the state court itself transfers it
options.misconception: requires the state court to initiate removal

options.text: Removal is automatic once the amount in controversy is large enough
options.misconception: ignores the diversity requirements

questions.explanation: Removal depends on satisfying the federal jurisdictional requirements, including complete diversity and a sufficient amount in controversy, and it is not automatic. The state court then decides whether to transfer the case.
questions.hint: Check whether every federal requirement is met.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rationale for special three-judge panels.
questions.stem: The planner asks why special panels were created for some statutory challenges. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: The special panel was created to add judicial weight and independence to challenges that can affect the operation of state law across an entire jurisdiction, because a single district judge bound by precedent of the circuit could handle such a case alone. A panel of one circuit judge and two district judges, drawn from outside the district's ordinary pool, reduces the chance that one local judge decides a question of broad reach, and direct appeal to the Supreme Court gives such cases a shorter route to high review.

questions.explanation: Special panels add judges from outside the local district and give broad statutory challenges a shorter route to high review. Ordinary single judge practice would leave such cases to one local judge.
questions.hint: Consider why one local judge is inadequate for broad challenges.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the judges needed to dispose of an expected caseload.
questions.stem: The planner's capacity note says a district received 7,200 new filings in a quarter and expects 12,000 for the following quarter. If the district's judges can dispose of 240 cases per judge each quarter, how many judges would be needed to dispose of the 12,000 filings in a quarter?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
questions.learningObjective: Explain why few ordinary disputes begin in the Supreme Court.
questions.stem: While revising the transit corridor map, the planner asks why so few disputes reach the Court for trial. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: The Supreme Court is a court of limited original jurisdiction, meaning it will begin a case only when it fits one of the categories the Constitution sets out, chiefly controversies between two or more states and suits against a state by citizens of another state. Most disputes instead begin in a trial court and reach the Court only through discretionary review, which explains why the volume of original matters in a term is small compared with the number of cases denied review.

questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction covers a few defined categories, so most disputes begin elsewhere and arrive only if the Court grants review. The small number of original cases follows from that structure.
questions.hint: Focus on the limited list of categories the Court may begin.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of the quorum rule.
questions.stem: During a site review, the planner asks what the quorum rule is for. Which answer is best?

answer.exemplar: The quorum rule lets the Court transact business with a smaller number of members than the full Court, which matters when several seats are vacant or justices are recused. A quorum of six lets the Court convene, hear argument, and handle routine matters, while the separate requirement of enough members to decide a case protects against deciding major questions with too few members present, so the two rules serve different purposes.

questions.explanation: The quorum rule allows the Court to function when fewer than nine members are available, and it is paired with a higher number required for decisions. The two rules serve different purposes.
questions.hint: Consider what the rule allows when seats are vacant.
